statement: Spider Woman/Spider Grandmother figures appear across multiple Southwestern traditions — Diné Naʼashjéʼii Asdzą́ą́, Hopi Kokyangwuti, and Keresan Pueblo Thought Woman (Tse-che-nako/Sussistanako) — but specialists document a real functional difference rather than treating this as simple shared borrowing: in Hopi tradition Spider Grandmother is a CREATOR figure (creator of humans/all living things), whereas in Diné tradition Spider Woman is explicitly NOT the creator of humans, functioning instead as a constant helper/benefactor/culture-teacher credited with teaching weaving. In some recorded Navajo tellings Spider Woman is herself described as a Kisani (Pueblo) woman taught weaving by a spider — the tradition's own internal narrative gestures toward a Puebloan point of origin for the weaving-teaching motif, consistent with the broader documented pattern of post-1680 Puebloan-Navajo religious exchange, though no named specialist source explicitly asserting "Spider Woman was borrowed from Pueblo religion" as a direct causal claim was located in this research pass.

sources.citation: General comparative sourcing on Spider Woman/Spider Grandmother across Diné, Hopi, and Keresan traditions (Encyclopedia.com "Spider Woman"; native-languages.org "Spider Woman, the Navajo goddess").

does_not_demonstrate: That Spider Woman was directly borrowed from Hopi/Keresan tradition into Diné tradition, as opposed to two independently documented adjacent facts (the shared-figure pattern and the general post-1680 contact/exchange pattern) that this project connects only as inference
